chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
title: Gangsters and Chicago clubs: Capone's Radio Inn
summary: Collins says gangster-owned clubs gave musicians work and sometimes shooting, and the Radio Inn was rumored to be Capone's.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Yeah, Wendell Phillips, yes. So after that, as I told you, I was working with my mother on the north side of Chicago. Gangsterland. And --
The gangsters though supported a lot of jazz (inaudible), I mean because --
They sure did, yeah. Because of the gangsters' Clubs
(Inaudible) there was a lot of work for them, wasn't there.
Isn't that the way it worked?
Yes, as a matter of fact there was always

rumor at this club I played, the radio end, with Elbert Topps -- Elbert Topps, was owned by Capone. You know. But most of the clubs at that time was all the gansters would hang out in there, you know.
Evidently, you know. We -- and sometimes it was pretty rocky, you know, they'd get to fighting and shooting in there, and all you could do was get out. You know, seriously, yeah.

Oh, no, you hid behind the piano or got out or did whatever you could to get out of there, because they weren't kidding, you know. It was frightening, really. But Chicago at that time was pretty frightening place. But there was always a lot of graft, so consequently there was always clubs, music, you know, some money to be made. You could make some money, you know. Not a lot but enough to sustain you.
Did they pay better than other places?
